title: Part I
author: David Hume
summary: Demea explains why he teaches his children natural theology last. Philo welcomes this, on the grounds that reason is too weak to reach so far, and Cleanthes asks whether a sceptic can really live by his doubts. The three then debate whether religion has gained more from scepticism or from reason.

notes.note: Pamphilus, the narrator, is Cleanthes's pupil; he listens but takes no part in the argument.

notes.on: last of all the Nature of the Gods
notes.note: Hume's note: Chrysippus, the third head of the Stoic school, as quoted by Plutarch in *On Stoic Self-Contradictions* (*De Stoicorum repugnantiis*).
A transcription error: the 1779 printing reads *study and inquiry*.
Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BC), the founder of Stoicism.

notes.on: Vain Wisdom all and false Philosophy
notes.note: Milton, *Paradise Lost*, ii. 565–569, of the fallen angels' philosophising.
Hume's note: *L'art de penser*, that is *La Logique, ou l'art de penser* (1662), the 'Port-Royal Logic' of Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole.

Hume's note: Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), Bishop of Avranches, author of the *Demonstratio evangelica* (1679) and of the sceptical *Traité philosophique de la foiblesse de l'esprit humain* (published 1723).

notes.on: the excellent saying of Lord Bacon
notes.note: Francis Bacon, *Essays*, 'Of Atheism': 'a little philosophy inclineth man's mind to atheism; but depth in philosophy bringeth men's minds about to religion.'
